title: Every Writer Supported: A Baltimore Curriculum Project Teacher on DI Language Programs di-language-programs/
author: Zach Groshell
source: educationrickshaw.com (Education Rickshaw, Direct Instruction Podcast), October 21, 2026
summary: In this Direct Instruction Podcast interview, with a full transcript on the page, Zach Groshell talks with Baltimore Curriculum Project teacher Jared Brewer about how DI builds writing. Brewer explains that the lower levels teach sentence structure and short paragraphs, with second graders writing four to six sentence paragraphs, and that by fourth grade students write nearly complete essays. Because small skills such as punctuation and capitalization are taught earlier, the long drafting and publishing project applies skills rather than starting from nothing. Groshell contrasts this with make-up-your-own-prompt writing, which split classes into prolific writers and strugglers, whereas a step ladder supports everyone. Brewer says the main takeaways from the conference are a specific routine for active monitoring and shared paragraph-grading standards across grades.
points: Brewer describes DI writing as a progression from sentence structure and short paragraphs in early levels to near-complete essays by fourth grade.
Earlier mastery of punctuation and capitalization lets the drafting and publishing of a long piece apply practiced skills.
Groshell contrasts the structured path with open prompts, which tend to split a class between prolific writers and strugglers.
Brewer values DI's specific approach to active monitoring, which makes sure every student gets teacher time during independent work.
Shared paragraph-grading standards give consistency from grade to grade because teachers otherwise dock different errors.
quotes: But we often don't associate DI with the careful teaching of language.

In the second-grade curriculum, they're responsible for writing anywhere from four- to six-sentence paragraphs. As you go up, in what I've seen in the fourth-grade curriculum, there's almost complete essay writing.
And I think the publishing step is really positive for them, because they can see a final piece that they've done.
So the class became kind of bifurcated: who wrote the most at home, maybe, and then who struggled.
In this case, because everyone's moving up that step ladder, they're supported.
Paragraph grading is something we all do differently. None of us are going to think the same things should be docked or considered an error in the same ways.
making sure I'm consistent, so every student gets some of my time during their independent work period
